text: Investment strategy for 2H26: Proposing stock strategies for both risk-on and risk-off markets

In this report, we update our Asia Technology team's investment strategy, focus areas, and recommended stocks for the second half of 2026. In 1H26, AI server/DC-related hardware stocks were key drivers of share prices, and the scope of stock picking expanded to areas such as electronic components and electronic materials. Heading into 2H26, meanwhile, we present several stock strategies amid the highly volatile environment, such as stock selection for risk-on markets and defensive plays for risk-off markets. Our three key messages are as follows:

(1) Maintaining a fundamentally bullish view on Asia AI server/DC-related (hardware) stocks: We expect demand to continue to outpace supply and high value-added technology to continue to outweigh cost-reducing trends. We believe the current AI-driven cycle remains large and long. Although related stocks have seen profit-taking entering July, we view this as a healthy adjustment following the rapid share price surge.
(2) Criteria for selecting AI server/DC-related stocks: We consider the following two criteria for stock selection in risk-on markets.

Sub-segments: Compared to previous expectations, we expect extended tightness in major sub-segments like memory. text: 2H26: Three key messages and stock recommendations
In this report, we update our investment strategy, focus areas, and stock recommendations across the Asia technology team coverage for 2H26.

In our January 12 report, Asia Tech Outlook & Resurgent Japan - Seizing the Global Growth Opportunity: A broader and deeper AI presence in the Asian supply chain, we highlighted five themes we believe are under the market's radar in the AI space:
■ Extensive business opportunities driven by soaring power consumption
■ Extensive business opportunities driven by faster large-scale data transmission
While these five focus areas remain unchanged, given the significant share price fluctuations YTD we now present three perspectives for 2H26 and update our stock recommendations.

1. We remain bullish on fundamentals/share prices in the Asia AI supply chain (hardware). The two bottom-up trends we monitor for AI server/data center (DC) applications driving the cycle—namely (1) signs of semiconductor/component device supply exceeding demand, and (2) signs of a shift toward lower cost trends over higher value-added technology (i.e., a slowdown in technological evolution)—have yet to materialize. Furthermore, beyond server (infrastructure) investment, the continued penetration of edge devices such as physical AI and edge AI could serve as the next driver. While share prices in the Asia AI supply chain (hardware) have risen significantly YTD, we maintain an overall bullish stance for 2H26, as we believe the AI cycle is still large and long.

2. Selecting AI stocks not only requires assessing expansion into sub-segments; well-regarded names require a closer examination of their individual risk-returns. Compared to previous expectations, we expect extended tightness in major sub-segments like memory. In addition, valuations of niche electronic components (such as MLCCs) and electronic materials rose in 1H 2026, and we see potential for supply/demand tightening to spill over into silicon wafers and analog/power semiconductors (excluding China) in 2H26. Shin-Etsu Chemical and SUMCO are key players in silicon wafers, alongside Renesas Electronics and Rohm in analog/power semiconductors.

Meanwhile, for sub-segments/companies where supply/demand is already tight (and share price valuations have advanced), we think assessing the risk-return of individual companies becomes even more crucial. Factors for analysis include: (1) significant benefits from higher prices/ASPs, (2) the ability to unlock capacity constraints through timely investments, (3) valuations lagging despite future profit contributions from AI, and (4) idiosyncratic drivers not priced into consensus. Accordingly, examining individual stock risk-returns, news flows, and timing in greater detail is critical. On July 6, we upgraded Nittobo to Buy from Neutral, driven by prolonged supply/demand tightness of
T-Glass and its positive impact on pricing/ASP (LINK). We evaluate other stocks such as Panasonic, Sumitomo Electric Industries, Lasertec, and Ebara, based on their individual risk-return profiles.

3. As a safety net in the event of a risk-off market, investors should consider stocks that are conversely starting to seize new business opportunities through AI disruption, by which we mean not only the varying degree of disruption, but also the threat of AI beginning to generate new demand for software/system construction, such as cyber solutions. Such stocks may be oversold and could attract attention as investment candidates if the main AI hardware names were to face a risk-off phase for any reason. Examples of stocks poised to benefit from generative AI include NRI, Baycurrent, NEC, Fujitsu, and Recruit.

text: Maintaining an overall bullish stance on the Asia AI supply chain (hardware) in 2H26

In our June 8 report (Japan Electronic Components/Semiconductors: Potential onset of one of the largest cycles in history), we highlighted the possibility that the sector is entering one of its largest cycles ever, driven by AI impacts. We also argued that we are likely currently in the early stages of this cycle.

The timing with which investors have begun to price the cycle into share valuations in the Japan electronic components/semiconductors sector has arrived about three years later than for the main Asia AI hardware sectors such as foundries, memory, and SPE (hence our use of “early stages”). However, even in the leading sectors, we see absolutely no sign of a peaking-out at present. Rather, over the past six months, our analysts covering Asia technology (hardware) have become increasingly bullish on the outlook.
To detect a cycle peak-out, we will monitor for the following two phenomena, which have yet to emerge:

1. Signs of semiconductor/component device supply exceeding demand: currently we see no such signs (rather, our view is that an increasing number of segments are experiencing stronger supply/demand tightness and a continued favorable pricing environment)

2. Signs of a shift toward lower-cost trends from higher value-added technology (i.e., a slowdown in technological evolution): currently we see no such signs (rather, our view is that the pace of technological evolution remains significant and the trend toward higher value-add will continue for some time)

Furthermore, as also noted in our June 8 report, we think it is highly likely that after the demand growth/technological evolution for AI servers, the penetration of edge devices such as physical AI and edge AI will continue as the next driver of hardware demand. The possibility that this cycle will be one of the biggest and longest ever, combined with the lack of any signs of a peak-out, underpins our continued overall bullish stance on the Asia AI supply chain (hardware) for 2H26.

In the AI cycle, semiconductors (memory), semiconductors (logic), and SPE lead, followed by electronic components, with silicon wafers recovering/expanding with a lag. We expect the AI cycle to be large and long

Each stock must be examined individually and in detail, as this group may include stocks with high long-term growth visibility, leading blue-chip stocks within the sector, stocks with further significant pricing/ASP upside (point 1 above), and companies capable of unlocking future potential through capacity expansion (point 2 above).

text: Based on these perspectives, our analysts have updated their stock selections for 2H26. Please see our stock preferences within each individual analyst's coverage below.

Stock preferences: For Murata Mfg. (Buy, on CL) and Taiyo Yuden (Buy), we focus on the positive ASP impact (mix improvement) from AI server/DC-related MLCCs as well as the MLCC book-to-bill ratio in the near term. Regarding price hikes, while Yageo (Buy, covered by Chao Wang), whose mainstay is commodity MLCCs, is likely to push for them in 2H26, we think late 2026 to early 2027—when annual price negotiations for automotive applications and the 2027 outlook become clearer—will be an important period to gauge the feasibility of price hikes for Japanese makers as well. Meanwhile, for Ibiden (Buy), we focus on management decisions regarding additional capacity expansion (new plants). We expect positive news flows regarding pricing and capacity expansion to raise medium-to-long-term earnings expectations going forward, and think the company will solidify its core positioning.

We also believe there is growing scope for price increases in some analog and power semiconductors from tightening supply/demand heading into 2H26. We are increasing our focus on Renesas Electronics (Buy), given its low valuation and position as potential beneficiary of pricing, and Rohm (Buy), as we think that when excluding the value of its stake in Toshiba, the AI-related contribution (including SiC) to the company's standalone earnings is underappreciated. Looking further ahead, we also increase our focus on companies like MinebeaMitsumi (Buy), which benefits from demand for AI/DC bearings and humanoid robots, and lags in terms of valuation.

Stock preferences: We remain constructive on the silicon wafer sector, supported by robust volume growth, largely in 300mm wafers, driven by broad-based AI server demand and our outlook for meaningful price increases in the next round of LTAs. Among our preferred names, SUMCO, as a pure-play wafer supplier, is well positioned to benefit from rising demand for leading-edge logic applications and a more substantive round of price revisions expected from late 2027 to 2028, which should drive significant earnings growth. For Shin-Etsu Chemical, too, there is good visibility on medium- to long-term earnings expansion, supported by higher volumes and improved pricing in advanced memory applications, growth in leading-edge lithography materials such as photomask blanks, photoresists, and multilayer materials, and the full-scale ramp-up of product lines for AI servers including quartz cloth and optical fiber preforms.

We expect supply-demand conditions to remain tight across several key materials, including Low-CTE glass and ultra-thin copper foil for semiconductor packaging substrate CCLs, as well as Low-Dk glass and VSP copper foil for AI server motherboards. Reflecting our positive outlook for both near- and medium-term earnings, we reiterate our Buy rating on Mitsui Kinzoku and recently upgraded Nitto Boseki (Nittobo) to Buy. Key catalysts are likely to be announcements of capacity expansion projects and associated price increases in VSP copper foil for Mitsui Kinzoku and in T-glass for Nittobo. We also expect Resonac to meaningfully outperform full-year guidance as early as 2Q, supported by strong earnings across a broad range of semiconductor back-end materials, including CCL, NCF, TIM, and DFR. Finally, we reiterate our Buy rating on JX Advanced Metals. In addition to growth in semiconductor sputtering targets, magnetic-material targets, titanium copper products, and high-purity tantalum powder for tantalum capacitors, we see InP substrates as a compelling medium- to long-term growth driver following the company's announcement of an approximately tenfold capacity expansion.

Stock preferences: While the overall equipment market remains buoyant on the back of expanding AI semiconductor demand, from the perspective of individual stocks, we focus on two points: (1) whether a company can achieve sales growth above the sector average on factors including technological change, proprietary technologies, and market share gains, and (2) whether top-line strength leads to a significant improvement in profit margins. From this standpoint, in the SPE sector, we maintain our Buy ratings on Lasertec (expanding adoption of ACTIS at wafer fabs), Ebara (expanding application of CMP processes and market share gains), DISCO (multiple growth drivers, centered on advanced packaging), and Tokyo Electron (a product portfolio generating WFE-plus growth and initiatives to improve profit margins).

In the NAND market, while NAND demand for AI inference servers continues to expand, major memory makers are maintaining their priority on DRAM investment, so we expect prolonged tightness in the supply/demand balance. Against this backdrop, we upgraded Kioxia Holdings to Buy on May 31. We maintain our view that the NAND market is inherently a cyclical market, but we believe higher profit levels are sustainable compared with past cycles, and therefore still see further upside for the share price and multiples (even after the significant share price rally YTD).

Stock preferences: First, we select stocks from the perspective of growing profit exposure to AI-related products and valuations, highlighting Panasonic HD and Sumitomo Electric. For Panasonic Holdings, the proportion of profits from AI/DC-related products, including BBUs for generative AI data centers where it holds around an 80% global market share, is expected to expand from 27% in FY25 to 47% in FY28. Meanwhile, the company's FY2E P/E (LSEG basis) is 22X, making it undervalued for an AI stock in our view. Similarly, Sumitomo Electric looks set to see its proportion of profits from AI/DC-related products expand from 15% in FY25 to 42% in FY28, driven by expanded sales of optical fiber cables, increased production of optical connectors, and contributions from optical devices and InP substrates with high marginal profit ratios, and it also looks undervalued at an FY2E P/E of 23X. As earnings results ahead confirm a rising proportion of AI/DC-related profits, we expect the stock to trade at a higher multiple. Next, in optical products where supply/demand is tight, we maintain our bullish view on Fujikura, which has ample scope to invest in capacity expansion. Global supply/demand for optical fiber cables is tight, but Fujikura has already announced large-scale capital investments in Japan and the US, and has the strong financial base with which to support them. In order to retain flexibility in its capital investments, the company's policy is to avoid relying on subsidies that would impose restrictions on its investments.

Heading into the second half of the year, we believe the spotlight could gradually shift to stocks related to 800V DC power supply systems. Thus far, power equipment such as transformers has garnered attention from the perspective of supplying power to data centers (outside the data center), but at present, rapid technological changes are occurring inside the data center, and a shift to direct current and higher voltages is being considered to accommodate the increased power consumption of computing chips while suppressing the increase in current. Under this new architecture, products such as SSTs (Solid State Transformers) and rectifiers are gaining importance, and companies such as Mitsubishi Electric, Hitachi, and Fuji Electric could benefit. If plans for these architectures firm up in the second half of the year, this will likely become a key investment theme.

Stock preferences: We expect 2027 S/D for conventional DRAM, NAND, and HBM to be all tighter than 2026 and the tightness to extend into 2028, being the most severe memory shortage in history due to strong AI/server demand and limited supply growth. We believe tight industry S/D should help the memory companies to see an elevated level of earnings power for at least the next few years. Under increasing visibility of prolonged shortage, customers are actively asking for LTA, which includes a high level of binding commitments and guarantees sustainable margin. We expect an expansion of LTAs to enhance demand visibility for memory suppliers, leading them to make more

efficient capex plans and lower the oversupply risk that we have seen in the past. We expect Samsung Electronics (SEC) to be one of the key beneficiaries of conventional memory shortage, given its outsized exposure in this segment relative to peers. Adding the significant improvement in its HBM business that we expect from this year driven by stronger demand from ASIC customers and increased market share within Nvidia, we estimate 2026E OP will grow more than 8X yoy to reach over W370tn, and a historically high ROE of 52%. With this record profit and FCF generation, we also expect a material upside to the company's shareholder return as well.

In addition, we highlight Samsung Electro-Mechanics (SEMCO) as we expect the AI tailwinds to help the company to fire on all its cylinders, especially highlighting: 1) strong MLCC business from AI servers and auto, 2) new growth driver in silicon capacitors, and 3) significant growth in ABF substrates driven by favorable S/D and AI customer expansion. For MLCC, we expect AI server MLCC demand to remain strong due to solid AI server units growth and increase in MLCC content per server to accommodate higher power consumption. However on the supply side, only a few companies can manufacture AI server MLCC and as MLCC industry is already seeing 90+% UTR, we expect favorable S/D condition to benefit SEMCO. We expect SEMCO's AI server MLCC to see strong growth and as AI server MLCC is sold at double-digit times higher than standard MLCC with much higher margin, we expect increasing mix of AI server to drive MLCC ASP and margin higher. Regarding ABF substrate, we also expect the S/D outlook to be favorable for at least the next few years as AI server demand remains strong and larger design and higher layer count for AI substrate is tightening the supply. With industry-wide UTR reaching full level but limited capacity additions available in the near-to-mid term, we expect S/D to remain favorable and benefit SEMCO. We expect SEMCO ABF revenue to see strong growth and margin to also see meaningful improvement with higher server mix.

Stock preferences: AI continues to anchor our positive view on leading-edge foundry heading into 2027E and beyond, remaining the primary engine behind both advanced-node and advanced packaging demand. For TSMC (2330.TW), we look for another year of solid growth in 2026E with revenue (in USD terms) up 39% YoY on top of an already strong 2025 (36% YoY), underpinned by fully loaded N3/N5 utilization on resilient AI demand and ongoing productivity gains, a strong N2 revenue ramp, and robust advanced-packaging pull. Looking into 2027E, we expect TSMC to accelerate its N3 capacity expansion into 2027E – with N3 capacity reaching 200kwpm by end-2027E, as N3 is the key bottleneck for AI/HPC applications, reinforcing our conviction in a multi-year growth runway.

Away from foundry, we see a select group of covered AI names spanning ASIC, advanced packaging and testing as well placed for strong 2026E growth, as rising AI chip volumes, larger package sizes, longer test times, higher TDP, and wider SLT adoption all play to their strengths. Our preferred Buy-rated exposures are 1) MediaTek (2454.TW), our key AI ASIC play, where an accelerating AI ASIC ramp with much stronger shipments should drive a sharper earnings inflection into 2027E. We expect MediaTek's AI ASIC revenue to reach US\$2/20.25/52.5bn in 2026-28E, accounting for 9%/49%/70% of revenue, 2) Hon Precision (7769.TW), the dominant FT handler provider, which is set to benefit from growing handler/ATC demand with rising chip volumes and lengthening test times,

3) MPI (6223.TWO), where we expect strong AI ASIC probe card momentum into 2027E, with further upside from its emerging CPO test equipment opportunity, 4) WinWay (6515.TW), where robust CPU test socket demand – driven by agentic AI – adds to an accelerating structural TAM expansion that extends its growth visibility into 2030, and 5) Aspeed, for which we see a structurally stronger growth trajectory into 2028 driven by agentic AI demand, stronger AI ASIC momentum with market share gain, and accelerating penetration of the higher-ASP AST2700 generation.

Stock preferences: The CCL sector continues to benefit from ongoing CCL spec upgrades, while CCL supply remains structurally constrained (given >1 year expansion lead time). In terms of individual stocks, we focus on two factors: (1) pricing conditions of CCL, with CCL price hike expected to continue accelerating in 2H26, supporting GM/OPM, and (2) product mix shift towards the higher end, with M9 CCL expected to enter MP in 2H26, led by Nvidia being the first to adopt and followed by ASIC customers. From this perspective, we maintain our Buy rating for EMC (M9 CCL will contribute at least low single digits % of total revenue in 2026) and TUC (high-end product mix should continue to go up in 2H26 driven by ASIC customers).

In addition, we believe the overall ABF substrate industry has entered a solid pricing upcycle, NYPCB (Buy, on CL) will not only enjoy a solid pricing uptrend but also an increasing exposure to the high ASP/margin high end AI projects. For power, we expect AI PSU BOM cost per watt to increase for next gen AI server with higher power density (43% higher BOM per watt from 5.5kW PSU to 12kW PSU), and the adoption of power rack (+-400V / 800V) from late 2026 will also benefit Delta (Buy).
Taiwan Downstream Supply Chain (Allen Chang, Verena Jeng)

Stock preferences: We are positive on Taiwan AI server supply chain, supported by rising AI server racks: 55k/ 105k/ 163k in 2026-28E and growing ASIC adoption, with ASICs accounting for 50%/ 52%/ 55% of AI chips in 2026-28E. We expect the ongoing AI infrastructure cycle to support supply chain companies' growth through 2028E: US leading CSPs in aggregate capex is expected to grow at 76% YoY in 2026E (vs. 74% YoY in 2025) (Global Server TAM report link).

Among AI servers ODMs, we remain positive on Buy rated Hon Hai (on CL) / FII in US Cloud, given their strong R&D, comprehensive offerings (GPU module, baseboard, AI servers, CPU servers, CPO switch, liquid cooling, etc.), and global production sites. We see these strengths continuing to support market share gains amid rapid technology migration (Hon Hai / FII report link). We are also positive on Wiwynn's leading market position in ASIC AI servers and its diversification into GPU AI server racks, supported by strong demand from leading US CSPs across general servers and AI servers (Wiwynn report link).
Mainland China semis supply chain (Allen Chang, Verena Jeng)

Stock preferences: We are positive on the progress made by local memory and advanced logic suppliers in meeting rising demand from local CSP clients in China on generative AI demand; this is positive for China's semis supply chain across foundry, SPE, semi material, components, IP and design. Media reported that (Link) memory supplier
CXMT has signed a multi-year supply agreement with Tencent on server DRAM chips, and the reported value is worth more than Rmb20bn (China SPE report link).

We remain constructive on NAURA as the leading local SPE supplier offering comprehensive products while expanding into new categories and advanced node applications. With the accelerated adoption of local GPU chipsets in AI foundation models (e.g. BABA Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, SenseNova U1, etc.), we are positive on rising client demand for advanced node applications, benefiting local SPE suppliers including NAURA due to their strong R&D capabilities. We are constructive on Hua Hong's growth trajectory and margin improvement ahead, supported by growing semiconductor demand for AI applications and devices. Hua Hong continues to ramp the final capacities of its second 12 inch fab, and we expect construction of the company's new 12 inch fab to start soon, supporting rising client demand. (Hua Hong report link)
Could stocks perceived negatively by investors due to AI disruption fears become good investment candidates during a risk-off phase?

Here we introduce our views on companies that we feel have been perceived negatively by the equity market relative to their underlying capabilities, including those for which AI disruption is now conversely starting to open up new business opportunities. These stocks could gain attention as investment candidates if major AI hardware stocks were to face a risk-off phase for any reason.

While the degree of AI disruption varies across tech subsectors, on the flipside it is important to highlight that threats from advanced AI are starting to unearth new demand for software/system construction, including in cybersecurity applications.

While concerns over AI disruption linger, we are starting to see signs of recovery in the US in investor sentiment and US software stock indices, spurred by strong earnings from Snowflake and comments from Capgemini during its IR Day. Stock prices in the Japan IT services sector remain soft, likely facing headwinds from sector rotation. However, in light of the difference in customer in-sourcing rates between the Japanese and US markets, the view is spreading that major Japanese system integrators are less likely to be disrupted by AI. In recent discussions with investors, our impression is that excessive concerns over AI disruption are gradually receding. Headwinds from sector rotation could continue, but based on strong fundamentals, we watch closely for the timing of a stock price reversal. Following Accenture's earnings (June 18; see report), share prices across the entire sector fell the next day, and investor sentiment worsened further. However, the company's sluggish earnings were primarily driven by client investment restraint due to the situation in the Middle East, which has little impact on the demand environment for IT services in Japan, and we believe stocks are now looking even more undervalued. From the following two perspectives, we recommend NEC, Fujitsu, NOM Institute, and BayCurrent as Buy-rated stocks with the potential to benefit from the spread of generative AI.

In the short term, trends in AI-related business sales will likely gain attention as a catalyst for the IT services sector. The market consensus is that the spread of generative AI is a headwind for the IT services demand environment, but similar to the on-premise vs. cloud transition, generative AI is also creating new IT services demand. We believe that if this becomes visible in companies' earnings results, it will serve as a positive catalyst, increasing the possibility of a share price reversal for groups of stocks that benefit from AI.

According to NRI and Baycurrent (major consulting firms), AI-related business is beginning to take off as corporate appetite for AI investment grows. Inquiries are mainly strong for consulting/SI demand in the AI implementation support space, construction of AI data infrastructure, and security measures. In particular, there is a strong need for AI data infrastructure currently, with projects on the scale of several billions of yen beginning to increase depending on the project. Also, while the sales scale for consulting is still small, demand is rising rapidly, including for security solutions. In our view, this is
likely to lead to demand for revamping aging systems, from the perspective of linking them to AI and strengthening security (accelerating the modernization trend).

With the emergence of frontier AI models, significant security issues are coming to light, but similar to DX, a vertically integrated model of consulting followed by system development is likely to be effective in AI transformation (AX) as well. When companies make full-scale AI investments, the decision-making authority lies with management rather than the IT department. Thus, NRI, which has deep ties with customers' C-suite executives through its consulting business, is more likely to be able to win over customers than its competitors, in our view, and we consider it to be in an advantageous position. Baycurrent, as a pure-play consulting firm, should also benefit most from the expansion of consulting demand for AI implementation support and security solutions. Similar to NRI, NEC and Fujitsu operate across all areas, including consulting, SI, network construction, and security, so they could also see expanded demand for AI-related business.

The next catalyst to watch is profitability improvement through AI. As a measure to improve profitability, companies have indicated plans to focus on AI-driven development, which applies generative AI to system development, testing, and other functions. NEC, Fujitsu, and NRI have all entered into business alliances with Anthropic and expressed their intention to utilize its AI tool (Claude Code) for AI-driven development. At present, Fujitsu and Hitachi are leading the way in AI-driven development efforts, and this is already having a positive impact on their company-wide profits. Going forward, we expect NRI, which is proceeding with the full-scale roll-out of its proprietary AI-driven development platform, and NEC, which is advancing the internal use of Claude Code, to start to see AI-driven development benefits emerge.

NEC sees operational efficiency improvements via generative AI (including AI-driven development) as the biggest driver of profitability improvement in its IT services business. Fujitsu expects its gross margin to continue improving by +2 pp or more per year from FY25 through FY35, driven by the full-scale roll-out of AI-driven development and personnel optimization. We believe both companies will see a significant profit uplift from expansion in the scope of AI-driven development, given the large scale of their IT services businesses. NRI's medium-term plan also assumes a profit increase of c.¥15 bn over the next three years from operational efficiency improvements, including AI-driven development. According to the company, development automation by AI agents is progressing ahead of its expectations, boosting the possibility of further benefits.

text: Regarding the impact of generative AI on Japan's game & internet sector, we get the impression that objective scrutiny is progressing away from one-sided discussions of AI disruption. We are starting to see a gradation of effects: (1) Generative AI has a positive impact: Recruit Holdings (Buy); (2) Limited negative impact from generative AI from a creative perspective, with potential benefits in terms of production efficiency: Game sector; (3) Generative AI could have a negative impact and requires close monitoring: Internet advertising space and ad agencies. We believe we are entering a phase of further stock differentiation. We highlight Recruit Holdings, Capcom, and Sony Group as Buy-rated beneficiaries.

Compared with the entertainment sector, the impact of generative AI on Japan's internet sector is becoming event in the underlying business environment and earnings in a shorter timespan, and both positives and negatives have come into sharper focus. Representative of the positive side is Recruit Holdings' Indeed business. The use of AI to enable rapid and advanced matching of companies and job seekers (expanded use of Premium Sponsored Jobs and more advanced screening) is driving monetization, resulting in higher US ARPJ (US Average Revenue Per Job posting: up +25% yoy in 4Q3/26, and we estimate +21% yoy in FY3/27). Recognition of Indeed being well-placed to benefit from AI is spreading in the equity market, and we expect Recruit Holdings to continue to be preferred within the sector.

At the same time, LY Corp (Not Rated) could be susceptible to negative impacts from generative AI. While the company is actively utilizing generative AI, including the introduction of an AI agent named Agent i, it could face direct competition from generative AI in the search domain. Indeed, its daily unique browser count (quarterly average) declined by -3.5% yoy in 4Q3/26. In addition, ad placement on generative AI platforms is starting gradually in various countries, and ad placement on ChatGPT was recently launched in Japan as well. Three companies—CyberAgent, Dentsu, and Hakuhodo—are serving as agencies for this ad placement, and for ad agencies, we believe now is a time where their ability to adapt business models to the generative AI era will be tested.

Investor concerns that generative AI will impair content scarcity and creative value have largely receded, in our view. Rather, the positive aspects of generative AI are becoming evident. These include SIE (Sony Interactive Entertainment) utilizing its internally developed AI tool Mockingbird (which automatically generates high-quality 3D facial animations from performance capture data) to achieve operational efficiencies in the creation of Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered, and Sony Group seeking out potential in utilizing AI for monetization, such as in payment processing fraud detection and user data analysis in its PlayStation Store.

Meanwhile, ongoing capital inflows into AI-related stocks—amid further outflows from Japan’s game & internet sector—remain a headwind for supply/demand. Under such conditions, we think stocks with strong earnings momentum which have undergone some adjustment in valuation look attractive. Among platformers, we highlight Sony Group (Buy; we estimate FY3/27 OP growth of +14% yoy, while FY3/27E P/E of 16.8X is near the bottom of its 5-year range). Among publishers, we highlight Capcom (Buy; we estimate FY3/27 OP growth of +16% yoy, while FY3/27E P/E has fallen back in line with the sector average at 21.3X despite the company’s commitment to double-digit (%) OP growth each year).

The GS Factor Profile provides investment context for a stock by comparing key attributes to the market (i.e. our universe of rated stocks) and its sector peers. The four key attributes depicted are: Growth, Financial Returns, Multiple (e.g. valuation) and Integrated (a composite of Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple). Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple are calculated by using normalized ranks for specific metrics for each stock. The normalized ranks for the metrics are then averaged and converted into percentiles for the relevant attribute. The precise calculation of each metric may vary depending on the fiscal year, industry and region, but the standard approach is as follows:

Growth is based on a stock's forward-looking sales growth, EBITDA growth and EPS growth (for financial stocks, only EPS and sales growth), with a higher percentile indicating a higher growth company. Financial Returns is based on a stock's forward-looking ROE, ROCE and CROCI (for financial stocks, only ROE), with a higher percentile indicating a company with higher financial returns. Multiple is based on a stock's forward-looking P/E, P/B, price/dividend (P/D), EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF and EV/Debt Adjusted Cash Flow (DACF) (for financial stocks, only P/E, P/B and P/D), with a higher percentile indicating a stock trading at a higher multiple. The Integrated percentile is calculated as the average of the Growth percentile, Financial Returns percentile and (100% - Multiple percentile).

Financial Returns and Multiple use the GS analyst forecasts at the fiscal year-end at least three quarters in the future. Growth uses inputs for the fiscal year at least seven quarters in the future compared with the year at least three quarters in the future (on a per-share basis for all metrics).
For a more detailed description of how we calculate the GS Factor Profile, please contact your GS representative.

Across our global coverage, we examine stocks using an M&A framework, considering both qualitative factors and quantitative factors (which may vary across sectors and regions) to incorporate the potential that certain companies could be acquired. We then assign a M&A rank as a means of scoring companies under our rated coverage from 1 to 3, with 1 representing high (30%-50%) probability of the company becoming an acquisition target, 2 representing medium (15%-30%) probability and 3 representing low (0%-15%) probability. For companies ranked 1 or 2, in line with our standard departmental guidelines we incorporate an M&A component into our target price. M&A rank of 3 is considered immaterial and therefore does not factor into our price target, and may or may not be discussed in research.
